content.title: Toilet checks, conflict resolution: Meet Artemis II crew and their jobs
content.text: April 1, 2026, 11:00 a.m. ETThey've worked their whole lives for a trip around the moon.The four astronauts in the Artemis II crew are set to lift off from Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Wednesday, April 1, for a historic lunar mission. The crew of NASA's first human moon mission in more than 50 years will break through more than the atmosphere: Among the Artemis II crew will be the first Black man, the first woman and the first Canadian to ever fly on a moon mission.When they launch, the Artemis II crew will be the first astronauts to fly aboard the space agency's Orion capsule, which will hitch a ride to orbit atop the towering Space Launch System. The crew won't be landing on the moon. But their expected 10-day trip mission is critical for lunar walks as soon as 2028.Meet the astronauts inside Orion and their expected roles during the spaceflight.Commander Reid WisemanAs commander, 50-year-old Reid Wiseman is the astronaut who ensures all facets of the mission work seamlessly, from crew communication to decisions made during spaceflight. Wiseman directs spaceflight with the pilot and is the main astronaut talking to Mission Control back on Earth, according to NASA.Wiseman is like a team manager, speaking for the astronauts to engineers back home or helping resolve questions or conflict among the crew during the mission, according to NASA. In the case of any indecision, the call will ultimately go to Wiseman.A decorated veteran Navy aviator, Wiseman served on two deployments to the Middle East and trained as a test pilot before he was selected as a NASA astronaut in 2009.Wiseman has been to space one other time. In 2014, he spent about six months at the International Space Station, where he completed two spacewalks and helped the crew set a station record by completing 82 hours of research in a single week.Wiseman, a Baltimore native, is a single father of two children, having lost his wife Carroll Taylor Wiseman in 2020 to cancer.Pilot Victor GloverPilot Victor Glover, 49, plays an essential role during Artemis II's ascent and entry, manually piloting the spacecraft and taking charge of flight information, according to NASA. Glover will coordinate with Wiseman to steer the spacecraft.Glover will be following mission instructions very closely and making sure the capsule stays on track as it orbits the moon."It is important for the pilot to follow protocol exactly and establish best practices, with consistency being key," says NASA's readout on Artemis II's roles.Glover can step in to help with other duties as needed and is the second in command who is prepared to lead the mission if necessary.A Navy aviator and test pilot, Glover was the pilot for the Crew-1 mission to the International Space Station. Launching in November 2020, the six-month mission was the first to the orbital outpost after the Dragon crew capsule was certified for spaceflight under a partnership between NASA and SpaceX.The mission was the first and only spaceflight for Glover, who was selected as a NASA astronaut in 2013 while serving as a legislative fellow in the U.S. Senate.Glover accumulated 3,500 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier-arrested landings and 24 combat missions, according to his NASA biography.Glover, a native of Pomona, California, holds several master's degrees and is married with four daughters.Mission specialist Christina KochChristina Koch has record-setting astronaut career leading up to Artemis II.Koch is an engineer and was selected to be an astronaut in 2013. She made history in 2019 when she conducted the first all-woman spacewalk at the International Space Station. On Oct. 28, 2019, Koch spent more than seven hours suited up and exposed to the vacuum of space with astronaut Jessica Meir, who is at the outpost again as part of the Crew-12 mission.Koch spent almost all of 2019 in space during her first and only mission yet, setting a record for the longest spaceflight for any American woman at 328 days. Just three other NASA astronauts have been on longer single missions.Koch, 47, is a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, and grew up in Jacksonville, North Carolina. She holds both a master's and a bachelor's degree from North Carolina State University in Raleigh, North Carolina. Her NASA biography reveals she has a long list of favorite activities including photography, surfing and rock climbing.As Mission Specialist 1, Koch's role is both scientific and technical. She is a highly trained expert and permanent astronaut corps member who will be tasked with carrying out Artemis II's operations. Koch will be seated closest to the spacecraft side hatch and will be the point person on hatch systems and operations, according to NASA. And yes, astronauts need to use the bathroom, too: Koch will set up the toilet system for testing after getting to orbit.Mission specialist Jeremy HansenCanadian Jeremy Hansen, 50, is Mission Specialist 2 on Artemis II. He'll be tasked on the first day with the initial checkout of life support infrastructure, such as Orion’s drinking water and emergency equipment, according to NASA. This role is also responsible for operating the docking hatch after splashdown in the case of an emergency.As mission specialists, both Hansen and Koch are staged to assist with "correction burns" when the spacecraft has to thrust to get back on track during the mission, according to NASA. These adjustments are largely scheduled.The mission specialists largely keep eyes out and ensure all available options are explored when when the crew makes a decision. Hansen, as well as Koch, is trained to step into commander or pilot duties if needed.Hansen is the only Artemis II crew member who will be making his first voyage to space. With a background as a fighter pilot, Hansen was selected in 2009 for astronaut training with the Canadian Space Agency. Among his credentials, Hansen in 2017 became the only Canadian to lead a new group of NASA astronaut recruits.A husband with three children, Hansen was raised on a farm in Ontario.How to tune into the launchA two-hour launch window opens on April 1 at 6:24 p.m. ET. Tune into all-day coverage by NASA on April 1 of Artemis II preparations leading up to the launch.Livestreams will be available throughout the day on Amazon Prime, NASA's YouTube channel and NASA+, the agency's free streaming service.
